tasks.title: Confirm Python 3 is installed and check the version from the terminal.
Write a file called hello.py that prints two lines, and run it with python3.
Write down two differences you noticed between running a Python file and a bash script.
Create a variable of each type: text, whole number, decimal number and true or false.
Use the type function to print the type of each variable.
Note that Python needs no dollar sign and no quotes rule like bash, and write down the difference.
Print a sentence that includes a variable using an f-string.
Use upper, lower, strip and split on a string and print each result.
Split a file path on the slash character and print the last part.
Ask the user for their name with input and greet them.
Ask for a number, convert it from text to a number, and double it.
Break it: type a word when it asks for a number and read the error message carefully.
Write a program that checks a number and prints whether it is above or below ten.
Add an elif branch so it also handles exactly ten.
Break it: remove an indent and read the error. Indentation is syntax in Python.
Create a list of five server names and print the whole list.
Print the first item, the last item, and the first three items.
Add an item, remove an item, and print how many items remain.
Loop over your list of servers and print each one on its own line.
Inside the loop, print a different message for names that start with a chosen letter.
Count how many items matched and print the total after the loop.
Use range in a for loop to print the numbers one to ten.
Write a while loop that stops when a counter reaches five.
Use break to stop a loop early and continue to skip one item.
Create a dictionary describing a server with name, ip and status keys.
Read one value, change one value, and add a new key.
Loop over the dictionary and print each key with its value.
Create a list of three server dictionaries.
Loop over the list and print the name and status of each server.
Print only the servers whose status is not running.
Write a function that prints a greeting and call it three times.
Add an argument so it greets whatever name you pass in.
Rewrite one of your earlier programs so its main logic sits inside a function.
Write a function that returns a value instead of printing it, and store the result.
Give one argument a default value and call the function both with and without it.
Write a function that takes a server dictionary and returns True if it is running.
Import the os module and read an environment variable from Python.
Provide a default so the program still works when the variable is not set.
Move a hardcoded value out of one of your scripts into an environment variable.
Import and use two standard library modules, such as datetime and random.
Move a function into its own file and import it from another file.
Write down why splitting code into files matters once a program grows.
Cause an error on purpose and read the traceback from the bottom line upwards.
Wrap a risky operation in try and except so the program handles the failure.
Catch one specific error type rather than catching everything, and explain why that is better.
Open a text file and print its whole contents.
Read the file line by line and print each line with a number.
Use a with block so the file closes automatically, and explain what that protects against.
Write three lines into a new file and confirm the contents from the terminal.
Append a line without erasing the file, and note this matches redirection in bash.
Write a program that loops over your server list and writes a report file.
Read a JSON file into Python and print one value from it.
Reach a value inside a nested structure two levels deep.
Write a Python dictionary out to a JSON file, formatted so a human can read it.
Read an argument passed to your Python script from the command line.
Print a usage message and exit if the argument is missing.
Exit with a non zero code on failure so bash and CI can detect it.
Choose a small real job, such as summarising a JSON file or renaming files in a folder.
Write it with a function, an argument, and error handling.
Run it twice and confirm the second run causes no harm.
Add print statements to find out where a broken program goes wrong.
Learn what NameError, TypeError, KeyError and IndexError each mean by causing all four.
Write a short debugging checklist for Python and add it to your notes.
Write a test function that checks one of your functions returns the expected value.
Install pytest, run it, and watch the test pass.
Break the function on purpose and confirm the test catches it.
Rename the variables in one old script so each name says what it holds.
Split one long function into two smaller ones that each do one thing.
Add a short docstring to each function saying what it does.
Write a program that reads a log file passed as an argument.
Count how many lines are errors, warnings and info, then print the totals.
Print the five most common error messages with their counts.
Add two tests for your log parser and make them pass.
Handle the case where the file does not exist, with a clear message and a non zero exit.
Write a short README explaining what it does and how to run it.
Commit it to the repository alongside your Month 4 pipeline work.

questions.prompt: How do you run a Python file from the terminal?
questions.explanation: You call the interpreter and give it the filename, just as you did with bash.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a Python string?
questions.explanation: Text in quotes is a string, while the others are a number, a decimal and a boolean.

questions.prompt: How do you find out what type a variable holds?
questions.explanation: The type function is the quickest way to see what you actually have.

questions.prompt: What is an f-string used for?
options: Putting variable values inside a string
questions.explanation: It is the clearest way to build a sentence that includes a value.

questions.prompt: What does the split method do to a string?
options: Breaks it into a list of pieces
questions.explanation: You choose the separator, and it returns a list of the parts.

questions.prompt: What does the input function return?
questions.explanation: Even when the user types digits, you get text and must convert it yourself.

questions.prompt: What happens if you try to convert the word hello into a number?
questions.explanation: Python fails loudly rather than guessing, which is usually what you want.

questions.prompt: What is elif used for?
options: Checking another condition when the first was false
questions.explanation: It lets one chain handle several possibilities without nesting.

questions.prompt: What makes indentation different in Python compared to bash?
options: Indentation defines which lines belong to a block and is required
questions.explanation: A wrong indent is a syntax error, not just untidy formatting.

questions.prompt: How do you write a comment in Python?
questions.explanation: It is the same character bash uses for comments.

questions.prompt: Why does Python need no dollar sign to use a variable?
options: Because it is a programming language rather than a shell expanding text
questions.explanation: The shell substitutes text into commands, while Python works with values directly.

questions.prompt: What does the strip method do?
questions.explanation: It is essential when reading lines from a file, which always carry a newline.

questions.prompt: Python and bash both use a hash to start a comment.
questions.explanation: It is one of the few things that carries straight over from what you already know.

questions.prompt: Getting an error message means you have done something badly.
questions.explanation: Errors are information, and reading them properly is a skill worth building deliberately.

questions.prompt: Indentation in Python is optional styling.
questions.explanation: It defines the structure of your code, and getting it wrong stops the program running.

questions.prompt: How do you get the first item of a list?
questions.explanation: Python counts from zero, which catches everyone at least once.

questions.prompt: What does append do to a list?
options: Adds an item at the end
questions.explanation: It is the standard way to build a list up as a program runs.

questions.prompt: How do you find how many items a list holds?
questions.explanation: The len function works on lists, strings and dictionaries alike.

questions.prompt: What does a for loop do with a list?
options: Runs the block once for each item
questions.explanation: It is the same idea as the bash for loop you already know.

questions.prompt: What does range produce?
options: A sequence of numbers you can loop over
questions.explanation: It is how you loop a fixed number of times.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between break and continue?
options: break leaves the loop, continue skips to the next item
questions.explanation: One exits entirely and the other moves on.

questions.prompt: What is a dictionary?
options: A collection of key and value pairs
questions.explanation: You look values up by name rather than by position.

questions.prompt: How do you read a value from a dictionary?
questions.explanation: The key is the whole point, and it is what makes dictionaries useful for structured data.

questions.prompt: Why is a list of dictionaries a useful shape?
options: Because it matches how real data such as JSON is structured
questions.explanation: AWS responses, config files and APIs almost all look like this.

questions.prompt: How would you print only servers whose status is not running?
options: Loop over it and use an if inside
questions.explanation: Loop plus condition is the filtering pattern you will use constantly.

questions.prompt: What happens if you ask a dictionary for a key that does not exist?
questions.explanation: That error has a name, KeyError, and you will meet it often.

questions.prompt: Which bash idea does the Python for loop most resemble?
options: Looping over a list of items
questions.explanation: The syntax differs but the concept is identical to what you learned on day 11.

questions.prompt: Python lists are indexed starting from zero.
questions.explanation: It is the single most common early mistake, so it is worth saying out loud.

questions.prompt: A list of dictionaries is close to the shape of the JSON that AWS returns.
questions.explanation: That is exactly why this structure is worth being comfortable with before Month 6.

questions.prompt: You can loop over both a list and a dictionary in Python.
questions.explanation: Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys, and you can request values alongside them.

questions.prompt: Why put code inside a function?
options: So it can be reused and tested instead of repeated
questions.explanation: The same reason you wrote bash functions on day 27.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between printing a value and returning it?
options: Printing shows it, returning hands it back so other code can use it
questions.explanation: A function that only prints cannot be built upon.

questions.prompt: What is a default argument for?
options: So the function works without that argument being supplied
questions.explanation: It makes the common case simple while keeping flexibility.

questions.prompt: How do you read an environment variable in Python?
questions.explanation: It is the same idea as reading one in bash, through a standard module.

questions.prompt: Why give an environment variable a default in code?
options: So the program still runs when the variable is not set
questions.explanation: Missing configuration should not mean an immediate crash for a non essential value.

questions.prompt: Why move hardcoded values into the environment?
options: So the same code runs in different environments without editing
questions.explanation: This is the same principle as day 88 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What does import do?
options: Makes code from another module available in your program
questions.explanation: It is how you use the standard library and your own modules.

questions.prompt: Why split code into multiple files as it grows?
options: Because one long file becomes impossible to navigate and reuse
questions.explanation: The same reason you would not put every bash tool in one script.

questions.prompt: How should you read a Python traceback?
options: The last line first, then work upwards
questions.explanation: The last line names the error, and the lines above show how you got there.

questions.prompt: What does try and except do?
options: Lets you handle a failure instead of the program stopping
questions.explanation: It gives you a chance to respond rather than crash.

questions.prompt: Why catch a specific error rather than everything?
options: Because catching everything hides bugs you did not expect
questions.explanation: A broad catch turns a real problem into silent wrong behaviour.

questions.prompt: What does a KeyError usually mean?
options: You asked a dictionary for a key it does not have
questions.explanation: It is one of the four errors worth being able to recognise instantly.

questions.prompt: A function that returns a value is more useful than one that only prints.
questions.explanation: Returning lets other code make decisions with the result.

questions.prompt: Catching every possible exception with one broad except is good defensive programming.
questions.explanation: It hides bugs, and the failure then shows up somewhere far from its cause.

questions.prompt: Reading the traceback carefully is usually faster than guessing what went wrong.
questions.explanation: The traceback names the error and points at the line, which is most of the answer.

questions.prompt: Why use a with block when opening a file?
options: The file closes automatically even if an error occurs
questions.explanation: It is the same idea as trap and cleanup in bash on day 42.

questions.prompt: What happens when you write to a file that already exists?
options: It is overwritten unless you open it in append mode
questions.explanation: This mirrors the difference between one and two greater than signs in bash.

questions.prompt: Why read a file line by line rather than all at once?
options: Because a very large file may not fit comfortably in memory
questions.explanation: Log files in particular can be far larger than you expect.

questions.prompt: What does loading JSON into Python give you?
options: Dictionaries and lists you can work with directly
questions.explanation: This is why the nested data work on day 85 mattered.

questions.prompt: Why is Python better than bash and jq for complex JSON work?
options: Because nested logic and conditions get unreadable in a shell pipeline
questions.explanation: jq is excellent for simple extraction, and Python takes over when logic is involved.

questions.prompt: How do you read a command line argument in Python?
options: Through the argument list in the sys module
questions.explanation: It is the same concept as the numbered parameters in bash.

questions.prompt: What should a script do when a required argument is missing?
options: Print usage and exit with a non zero code
questions.explanation: Exactly the same rule you applied to your bash tools.

questions.prompt: Why does exiting with a non zero code matter for a Python script?
options: So bash, cron and CI can detect the failure
questions.explanation: The exit code is the interface between your script and everything that runs it.

questions.prompt: Why should a script be safe to run twice?
options: Because automation reruns things, and a second run should not cause damage
questions.explanation: The same idempotence principle from day 60 of the DevOps track.

questions.prompt: What makes a script genuinely useful rather than an exercise?
options: It does a real job you would otherwise do by hand
questions.explanation: Tools you use are the ones you remember and the ones worth showing.

questions.prompt: Why format JSON with indentation when writing it to a file?
options: So a human can read and review it
questions.explanation: Machine readable and human readable are both worth having when you can.

questions.prompt: What connects this month's Python to your Month 3 bash work?
options: Both handle JSON, arguments and exit codes, which is the shared interface
questions.explanation: The two tracks meet at the command line, which is why the conventions match.

questions.prompt: A with block protects you from leaving a file handle open after an error.
questions.explanation: It is automatic cleanup, and it is one of the first Python habits worth having.

questions.prompt: Python is always the right choice over bash for shell tasks.
questions.explanation: Short glue work stays in bash, and Python takes over when there is real logic or data handling.

questions.prompt: The usage message and exit code conventions carry over directly from your bash tools.
questions.explanation: That consistency is what lets your Python and bash tools be used together.

questions.prompt: What is a NameError usually telling you?
options: You used a variable or function name that does not exist
An index is out of range
questions.explanation: It is nearly always a typo or a name defined after it was used.

questions.prompt: What is a TypeError usually telling you?
options: You used a value in a way its type does not support
questions.explanation: Adding a number to a string is the classic example.

questions.prompt: What is an IndexError usually telling you?
options: You asked for a list position that does not exist
questions.explanation: It usually means an off by one mistake or an empty list.

questions.prompt: What does a test actually do for you?
options: Tells you when a change broke something that used to work
questions.explanation: Its value appears later, when you change something and want to know what you broke.

questions.prompt: Why deliberately break a function after writing a test for it?
options: To confirm the test actually catches the problem
questions.explanation: A test that passes no matter what is worse than no test at all.

questions.prompt: Why does a test that always passes give false confidence?
options: Because you believe you are protected when you are not
questions.explanation: It is the same problem as an alarm stuck on insufficient data.

questions.prompt: Why rename variables to say what they hold?
options: Because you will read the code far more often than you write it
questions.explanation: Future you is the main beneficiary of clear naming.

questions.prompt: Why split a long function into smaller ones?
options: Because each smaller piece is easier to understand and test
questions.explanation: A function doing three things is three functions waiting to be separated.

questions.prompt: What is a docstring for?
options: Saying what a function does, for whoever reads it next
questions.explanation: It sits with the code, so it is far more likely to stay accurate than a separate document.

questions.prompt: How should your log parser handle a file that does not exist?
options: Print a clear message and exit non zero
questions.explanation: A clear message beats a traceback for anyone who is not you.

questions.prompt: Why count the most common error messages rather than listing them all?
options: Because the frequent ones are usually the ones worth fixing
questions.explanation: It is the same reasoning behind alerting on thresholds rather than every single event.

questions.prompt: What should you have at the end of this month?
options: One small tool that works, is tested and is committed
questions.explanation: One working tool is worth more than twenty tutorial exercises.

questions.prompt: A test that passes even when the function is broken is worse than having no test.
questions.explanation: It creates confidence that is not backed by anything real.

questions.prompt: Handling a missing file with a clear message is part of writing a usable tool.
questions.explanation: The difference between a script and a tool is largely how it behaves when things go wrong.

questions.prompt: After one month of Python you should expect to be a competent programmer.
questions.explanation: You should expect to write small useful scripts, and real fluency takes considerably longer.
